newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien endures fierce election debate.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien endures fierce election debate.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien came under relentless attack on Monday from his four main opponents during the sole English-language debate of the federal election campaign.
"I expected that being the prime minister I'd be at the centre of attention, but it gave me a chance to respond," Chretien told reporters after the televised debate.

As the undisputed frontrunner in national polls and as the incumbent, he was the main target for the leaders of the other four main parties contesting the June 2 election, whether separatist or federalist, right-wing or socialist.

The 2-1/2-hour debate appeared to be less stage-managed than U.S. election debates and leaders openly attacked each other on issues ranging from health care cuts to the near victory by Quebec separatists in a referendum.

"You almost blew it, sir," Reform Party leader Preston Manning told Chretien, referring to the October 1995 Quebec vote, when the prime minister told Canadians not to worry. "You do not deserve a second chance."

Party leaders pointed out that during the last election, Chretien said in debates he would not cut health spending. He then slashed $7 billion Canadian ($5 billion U.S.) from health and social transfers to the provinces.
Chretien pointed out his government had pledged to restore some of the cuts because the light was visible at the end of the tunnel after years of slashing budget cuts.
"The light he saw at the end of the tunnel was the white of the eyes of the Canadian voter," said Conservative Party leader Jean Charest.

Leftist New Democratic Party leader Alexa McDonough charged that Chretien's Liberals had broken promises to scrap the hated federal Goods and Service Tax and not to cut health spending, and to make jobs the top priority.
"(And) he made a commitment to make jobs the number one priority. Canadians are still waiting," she said.
Gilles Duceppe of the Bloc Quebecois declared Quebec would soon be a sovereign country and then attacked the government's slow progress in reducing unemployment insurance premiums.
The 63-year-old leader, who did not speak in his native French language, tried to launch counter-attacks.

Addressing McDonough's goals for more spending, Chretien said it had been necessary to restore Canada's international financial position: "You won't have any social programmes in Canada if you have a bankrupt nation."
He said his vision for keeping Canada together was to work on problems one at a time.

The prime minister's strategists had pushed for an open debate format to try to erase the memory of a disastrous performance in a televised debate with ordinary Canadians in December, when Chretien denied breaking election promises.

Chretien went into Monday's debate with a lead of at least 20 points in the polls, which if they hold would give him a near sweep in the prize province of Ontario, with 103 of the 301 seats in the House of Commons, and return him to a majority government.

But he has faced criticism in central Canada for calling the election in the middle of flooding in Manitoba, blasts from the left for spending cuts and pressure from the Conservatives and Reform for tax cuts.
Pollsters also caution that Canadian voters have shown increasing volatility in recent years. Another debate was scheduled for Tuesday night, in French.
The emotional issue of Quebec and whether it should be an independent country was likely to figure more prominently during the French debate.
It was a declaration by Charest that he would hand a united Canada to his children that won the only applause of the evening.
"I intend to make this country work, because if there's one commitment I made to my children, it's that I'm going to pass on to them the country I received from my parents," he said.
